bib.title: Chain-of-Tools: Utilizing Massive Unseen Tools in the CoT Reasoning of Frozen Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Chain-of-Tools: Utilizing Massive Unseen Tools in the CoT Reasoning of Frozen Language Models", Mengsong Wu, Tong Zhu, Han Han, Xiang Zhang, Wenbiao Shao, Wenliang Chen (Soochow University). arXiv:2503.16779v1 [cs.CL], 21 Mar 2025. Preprint; no venue printed. Code and data: github.com/fairyshine/Chain-of-Tools.

COVERAGE: 43,164 of 43,164 chars read (all pages, including references and appendices A-E). Nothing skipped. Extraction of the figure plots is only axis numbers, so no curve values were readable.

FIT WARNING: Moderate to poor for a chapter on planning and tool use for agents. This is a research method for 7B open models. It trains small modules on hidden states (tool judge, query encoder, tool encoder) and picks tools by dot-product retrieval. It does not test API-style agents, in-context tool descriptions given to a strong model, cost, latency or tokens. There is no comparison against an in-context or description-retrieval baseline on the KBQA tasks. It is usable only as one worked example of "learned tool retrieval vs prompt-listing" with the caveats below. The cost claim is argued, not measured.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Claim: On a pool of 999 seen tools, CoTools picks the right tool more often than ToolkenGPT, and on 837 unseen tools ToolkenGPT scores 0.0% while CoTools scores 10.4%.
 number: seen 35.1 vs 23.8; unseen 10.4 vs 0.0 (top-5 unseen 33.68%)
 setup: STQuestions, LLaMA2-7B-Chat frozen, metric is tool-selection accuracy. Test set has 1,707 seen-tool and 1,066 unseen-tool questions. Single run.
 quote: "ToolkenGPT LLaMA 93.4 20.6 23.8 0.0 / CoTools(Ours) LLaMA 93.8 43.6 35.1 10.4"; "CoTools has a top1 accuracy of 10.41% and a top5 accuracy of 33.68%. ToolkenGPT has a top1 accuracy of 0.0%."
 where: Table 4 and Sec 4.3.3, about chars 20,000-26,000
2. Claim: Unseen-tool accuracy is low in absolute terms. Top-1 is about 10%, and the authors say that with synthetic training data the method is "still a long way from being usable".
 number: 10.4% top-1, 33.68% top-5
 setup: as above
 quote: "CoTools does much better though it is still a long way from being usable."
 where: Sec 4.2 after Table 4
3. Claim: With the 234 KAMEL tools and gold training data both methods are near ceiling. With ChatGPT-synthesised training data CoTools is far better.
 number: 93.8 vs 93.4 (sup); 43.6 vs 20.6 (syn)
 setup: KAMEL, 234 tools, LLaMA2-7B-Chat, 500 test items, selection accuracy. Single run.
 quote: "For cases with large amounts of gold training data such as KAMEL(sup), both methods perform well."
 where: Table 4 and Sec 4.3.1
4. Claim: At 1,000-tool scale CoTools still beats ToolkenGPT by more than 10 points. Top-5 for CoTools on KAMEL(sup) stays near 100%.
 number: ">10%" (value read from Fig. 6, not in text); "nearly 100%" top-5
 setup: STQuestions, 200 to 999 tools, LLaMA2-7B-Chat
 quote: "As the number of tools reaches a thousand scale, CoTools still outperforms the baseline by more than 10%."; "CoTools remains nearly 100% correct with the TOP 5 tools selected"
 where: Sec 4.3.2 and 4.3.1
5. Claim: On numerical reasoning with a Mistral-7B base, CoTools gives large gains over prompting. With LLaMA2-7B it is only about equal to ToolkenGPT, and multi-hop is near zero for all methods.
 number: GSM8K-XL 0.42 vs 0.14 (0-shot) and 0.10 (CoT) on Mistral; LLaMA 0.19 vs ToolkenGPT 0.18; FuncQA multi-hop 0.07 vs 0.06
 setup: GSM8K-XL (4 tools, 568 test), FuncQA (13 tools; 60 one-hop and 68 multi-hop test items). Single run per cell. Note that no ToolkenGPT run on Mistral is reported.
 quote: "CoTools(ours) Mistral 0.42 0.63 0.07"; "Every result is from a single run."
 where: Table 3, Sec 4.2
6. Claim: Performance depends on the base model. The method raises weak and strong models alike but does not close the gap.
 number: none
 quote: "The performance of CoTools is very dependent on the foundation model's own ability."
 where: Sec 4.2
7. Claim: ToolkenGPT, trained on seen tools, collapses onto a small group of seen tools when asked about unseen ones. CoTools does not show this pattern.
 number: none (read from Fig. 7)
 quote: "ToolkenGPT has a clear preference for a small group of tools however CoTools does not."
 where: Sec 4.3.3, Fig 7
8. Claim: A subset of hidden-state dimensions carries the tool-selection signal. Retrieving with only the 1,561 of 4,096 dimensions whose learned weight is above 1 costs 1.4 points of top-1.
 number: 1,561 of 4,096; top-1 down 1.4% from 93.8%; top-5 unchanged
 setup: KAMEL, LLaMA2-7B (d = 4096), Wdim learning rate 0.01
 quote: "At a learning rate of 0.01, 1561 of the 4096 dimensions are weighted more than the initial 1. We use only these dimensions for tool retrieval. The TOP1 accuracy has decreased by only 1.4% from the original 93.8%"
 where: Sec 4.3.4
9. Claim (design, no number): The tool is chosen by embedding similarity from name and description, not by listing tools in the prompt, so the prompt does not grow with the pool. The judge runs at every generated token. The ICL prompt is used only to fill in parameters.
 quote: "CoTools does not use the ICL prompt for tool selection, thereby enhancing efficiency in massive tool scenarios."
 where: Sec 2.1. The efficiency claim is not measured anywhere.

BASELINES (matched?)
- ToolkenGPT (LLaMA2-7B-Chat), the same training data and prompts. This is the closest match, on the benchmarks it created.
- 0-shot ChatGPT, 0-shot and CoT prompting of LLaMA2-7B and Mistral-7B. These appear on numerical tasks only. ChatGPT is a different, larger model, so it is not matched.
- On KBQA there is no prompting or in-context baseline: "Because of the large number of tools, we do not evaluate the Prompting method which is inefficient and hard to guarantee results." The paper's central contrast (in-context vs learned retrieval) is therefore not tested at scale.
- No external dense retriever (for example one on tool descriptions) is compared, though the paper says it avoids needing one.
- No ToolkenGPT on Mistral. All results are single runs with no variance. Prompts "provided in the dataset or baseline" are used.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: no tools with multiple return values; no large-scale real-world toolset (ToolBench is "too cumbersome and not well filtered"); existing tool datasets are "too simple or of low quality".
- Not shown: cost, latency or token savings (no measurement); end-to-end agent success on STQuestions (only selection accuracy); multi-turn or multi-tool planning; any model above 7B; comparison with in-context selection.
- STQuestions tools are Freebase relations, with questions rewritten by ChatGPT. This is a narrow relation-lookup task and not real APIs. Similar relations make it ambiguous.
- Training needs a fine-tuned judge and retriever per base model, and needs open-weight hidden-state access. This rules out closed API models.
- Dated: LLaMA2-7B, Mistral-7B v0.2 and ChatGPT baselines (2023-era). Modern native function calling and large-context models are not covered.
- The interpretability claim (key dimensions) is exploratory and shown on one dataset.
- Test split in Table 6 is garbled: FuncQA test shows "6068" (60 and 68).

BUILDS ON
ToolkenGPT (Hao et al., 2024), main baseline; datasets GSM8K-XL and FuncQA are from it. Toolformer (Schick et al., 2024); ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023b); API-Bank (Li et al., 2023); HuggingGPT (Shen et al., 2024); AgentBench (Liu et al., 2023); ToolDoc (Hsieh et al., 2023); Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023); Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2022b); Zero-shot CoT (Kojima et al., 2022); contrastive in-batch retriever training after DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); probing (Alain and Bengio, 2016); KAMEL (Kalo and Fichtel, 2022); SimpleQuestionsv2 (Weston et al., 2015).

CODE
No code in the paper (the repo is linked). The gated MLP used for judge and encoders (Eq 3, 6), as printed:
- J(h) = W_down((σ W_gate(h)) ⊗ W_up(h)), threshold θ = 0.5 (Sec 3.1)
- E_Q(h) = norm(Wdim ⊗ (h + E_Q'(h))) (Eq 6)
- Score_{Q,T} = V_Q · V_T; T* = argmax_T Score (Eq 9-10)
Tool prompt template (App. C): "tool name: [Tool Name], tool description: [Tool Description]"
KAMEL/STQuestions retrieval prompt: "Question: [Question] Answer: The answer is"
Hyperparameters (Table 5): Judge 3 epochs, lr 1e-5; Retriever 10 epochs, lr 1e-4, batch 16. Compute: 2 x V100 32G; about 2 hours per epoch for the GSM8K-XL retriever.

FIGURES (candidate)
Figure 2 (overview, p. 3): Tool Judge, Tool Retriever and Tool Calling pipeline. Query and answer fragment go to the frozen model, whose hidden state is encoded and dotted against tool vectors computed from name and description. It shows the in-context vs retrieved selection split in one picture. Alternative: Figure 6 (accuracy vs tool count, 200 to 999), which is the scaling evidence, but its values are not readable from the extraction. Figure 1 (ideal tool-calling flow, weather/schedule example) is a simpler teaching picture.
Run `scripts/papers/figures.py captions` to confirm page numbers. I did not run it.

PROBLEMS
- Figure plots and Table 6 are partly garbled in the extraction (Table 6 column merges, for example "19,0008,095" and "10,483 1,707 1,7071,066"). Fig 4-6 gains are quoted in prose only, so I could not read exact values.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
